Chapter 3: Journeys into the Heart of Nature
When the chance finally came to leave Europe behind, Alexander didn’t hesitate. The world outside everything he knew was calling—and he was ready to answer.
So, with a trusted friend by his side, he set off for South America—a place that, for most Europeans, was still wrapped in mystery and myth.
Just getting there was an adventure in itself. Crossing the Atlantic meant weeks at sea, facing wild storms and all kinds of uncertainty. But for Alexander, every single moment was a chance to notice, to learn, and to marvel at the world. He filled pages with detailed notes—everything from the changing color of the ocean to the patterns in the clouds overhead. To him, the world was bursting with hidden connections, and he was determined to find them.
Arriving in the tropics was like stepping into a dream. The forests teemed with life—plants and animals he’d never even imagined. The air was thick with the scent of flowers and the music of birds. Compared to the mild landscapes of Europe, it felt like he'd landed on another planet.
But Alexander wasn’t content to just stand back and admire the view. He wanted to understand how everything fit together. He climbed mountains, waded through rivers, and trekked deep into the jungles, collecting specimens and making careful measurements. He sought out local people, listening and learning from their deep knowledge of the land. He started to see how climate, altitude, and geography shaped every living thing—plants, animals, and even people.
One moment, in particular, really changed the way Alexander thought. While climbing a towering volcano, struggling through thin, icy air, he paused to look out over the landscape. What he saw took his breath away—not just the view, but the patterns. Different plants grew in distinct bands at different heights, each perfectly suited to its own environment. Suddenly, it was clear: nature isn’t random. It’s organized by invisible laws.
This wasn’t just a scientific finding. For Alexander, it was a revelation. Most people saw nature as a bunch of separate things. But he saw it all as one living, interconnected whole. The same patterns he spotted on a mountain in South America? They could be found in Europe, Asia, even Africa. The world was woven together by forces that crossed all borders and cultures.
Of course, the journey wasn’t easy. There were dangers everywhere—disease, wild animals, punishing weather. Supplies sometimes ran low, and the terrain could be brutal. But Alexander never lost his determination. Every hardship was a lesson, every setback a new chance to look deeper.
Along the way, he couldn’t ignore the realities of colonialism. He saw how European powers treated both the land and its people as things to be used and controlled. He listened to the stories of indigenous communities—people whose wisdom about the land was often ignored by outsiders. These experiences made a deep impression, strengthening his sense of justice and his belief in the value of every culture.
By the time Alexander returned to Europe, he’d gathered a mountain of data, specimens, and insights. But even more important, he’d developed a brand new way of seeing the world—one that recognized how everything is connected. His journey changed him forever. And soon, it would change the way everyone else understood nature, too.
